Mills|Janet Mills]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsME}} The '''2018 Maine gubernatorial election''' took place on November 6, 2018, to elect the [[governor of Maine]]. It occurred along with elections for the [[United States Senate election in Maine, 2018|U.S. Senate]], [[United States House of Representatives elections in Maine, 2018|U.S. House]], and other state and local elections. Incumbent [[Maine Republican Party|Republican]] Governor [[Paul LePage]] was term-limited and could not seek a third consecutive term. He later unsuccessfully sought a third term in [[2022 Maine gubernatorial election|2022]].{{Cite web |last=WMTW |date=2022-11-09 |title=Former Gov. LePage concedes, cites 'grave' concerns over inflation for Maine |url=https://www.wabi.tv/2022/11/09/former-gov-lepage-concedes-cites-grave-concerns-over-inflation-maine/ |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=www.wabi.tv |language=en}} This was one of eight Republican-held governorships up for election in a state carried by [[Hillary Clinton]] in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. The primaries for this election were the first in Maine to be conducted with [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked choice voting]] (RCV), as opposed to a simple plurality, after voters passed [[Maine Question 5, 2016|a citizen referendum]] approving the change in 2016.{{cite news|title=Maine became the first state in the country Tuesday to pass ranked choice voting|url=https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2016/11/10/maine-became-the-first-state-in-the-country-to-pass-ranked-choice-voting/|access-date=November 17, 2016|newspaper=Boston Globe|date=November 10, 2016|archive-date=November 16, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116075525/https://www.boston.com/news/politics/2016/11/10/maine-became-the-first-state-in-the-country-to-pass-ranked-choice-voting|url-status=live}} An [[advisory opinion]] by the [[Maine Supreme Judicial Court]] held that RCV would be unconstitutional for general elections for governor and the state legislature. The [[Maine Democratic Party|Democratic]] candidate was [[Maine Attorney General|Attorney General]] [[Janet T. Mills|Janet Mills]]. [[Maine State Treasurer|State Treasurer]] [[Terry Hayes (politician)|Terry Hayes]] and businessman Alan Caron had qualified for the ballot as independents, though Caron dropped out on October 29 and endorsed Mills. Former state senator and former mayor of [[Lewiston, Maine|Lewiston]] and [[Auburn, Maine|Auburn]] John Jenkins and perennial candidate Kenneth Capron ran write-in campaigns. Mills defeated Moody and Hayes with a majority to become the first female governor of Maine. This was the first election since [[2006 Maine gubernatorial election|2006]] that Maine elected a Democratic governor. Mills was also the first gubernatorial candidate to win at least 50% of the vote since [[Angus King]] in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1998|1998]], and the first non-incumbent to do so since [[Kenneth M. Curtis]] in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1966|1966]]. Mills received more votes for governor than any other candidate in Maine history, becoming the first Maine gubernatorial candidate to earn 300,000 votes. This was the first gubernatorial election since [[1982 Maine gubernatorial election|1982]] that a Democrat would win a majority of the popular vote.{{Cite web|url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=23&year=1982&off=5&elect=0|title=1982 Gubernatorial General Election Results - Maine|accessdate=April 4, 2023}} ==Background== Incumbent Republican [[Paul LePage]] was term-limited, having been elected twice consecutively in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 2010|2010]] and [[Maine gubernatorial election, 2014|2014]]. Woodbury]], former state senator == General election == After the primaries, most prediction models had the race as a tossup, noting Paul LePage's two victories and [[Hillary Clinton]]'s narrow margin of victory in the state in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. Others considered it to be a pick-up opportunity for the Democrats.{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2018/10/10/governors-seats-most-likely-flip-parties-november/?noredirect=on |title=The 10 governor's seats most likely to flip parties in November |last=Phillips |first=Amber |date=October 10, 2018 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-date=November 25, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125052217/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2018/10/10/governors-seats-most-likely-flip-parties-november/?noredirect=on |url-status=live }} Both Moody and Mills received the backing of outside money, with one PAC spending in excess of $1 million on television advertising in the state to support Mills's candidacy.{{Cite news |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2018/09/17/democratic-pac-tops-1-million-in-spending-in-governors-race/ |title=Democratic PAC tops $1 million in spending in Maine governor's race |last=Gallagher |first=Noel K. |date=September 17, 2018 |work=[[The Portland Press Herald]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181013093457/https://www.pressherald.com/2018/09/17/democratic-pac-tops-1-million-in-spending-in-governors-race/ |url-status=live }} On October 12, [[Jonathan Martin (journalist)|Jonathan Martin]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' published an article detailing a sex discrimination complaint filed against Moody and his business in 2006, which Moody settled for $20,000, resulting in the complaint being withdrawn. The complaint alleged that Moody went to the residence of a female employee and fired her for having a child just days after delivering the child via an emergency [[caesarean section]].{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/12/us/politics/shawn-moody-maine-discrimination.html |title=He Settled a Sex Discrimination Complaint. Now He Wants to Lead Maine. |last=Martin |first=Jonathan |date=October 12, 2018 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-date=October 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181012204634/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/12/us/politics/shawn-moody-maine-discrimination.html |url-status=live }} Moody denied the allegation through a spokesperson and later on Twitter.{{Cite news |url=https://www.wmtw.com/article/moody-responds-to-sex-discrimination-allegation-printed-in-new-york-times/23734297 |title=Moody responds to sex discrimination allegation printed in New York Times |last=Merrill |first=Paul |date=October 12, 2018 |work=[[WMTW (TV)|WMTW-TV]] |access-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-date=October 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181012154948/https://www.wmtw.com/article/moody-responds-to-sex-discrimination-allegation-printed-in-new-york-times/23734297 |url-status=live}} Though the first poll of the race saw Mills and Moody tied for first place with Hayes and Caron lagging behind, by the end of October, four different polls were released, each showing Mills with an eight-point lead over Moody. ''[[FiveThirtyEight]]'' declared the race "Likely D" when its gubernatorial projections were released in October, though other prediction models maintained the race as a tossup. On October 29, in a press conference at the main branch of the [[Portland Public Library]], Caron dropped out of the race and endorsed Mills. His name remained on the ballot, but any votes cast for him were regarded as blank.{{Cite news|url=https://bangordailynews.com/2018/10/29/politics/independent-alan-caron-quits-maine-governors-race/|title=Independent Alan Caron quits Maine governor's race|last=Shepherd|first=Michael|date=October 29, 2018|work=[[Bangor Daily News]]|access-date=October 29, 2018|archive-date=October 29, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181029232717/https://bangordailynews.com/2018/10/29/politics/independent-alan-caron-quits-maine-governors-race/|url-status=live}} Shortly before 10 pm on election night, Hayes conceded the race.{{Cite web |url=http://www.mainepublic.org/post/live-updates-democrat-janet-mills-becomes-maines-next-governor#stream/0 |title=Live Updates: Democrat Janet Mills Becomes Maine's Next Governor |date=November 6, 2018 |website=MainePublic.org |access-date=November 7, 2018 |archive-date=October 7, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007114641/https://www.mainepublic.org/politics/2018-11-06/election-night-2018-live-blog#stream/0 |url-status=live}} At 12:15 am on November 7, Moody conceded the race to Mills, and shortly thereafter Mills declared victory at Democratic headquarters in Portland. Mills became the first Maine gubernatorial candidate to receive more than 300,000 votes in a single election. Mills also became the first Maine gubernatorial candidate to win a majority of the vote since Angus King won nearly 59% of the vote in his re-election bid in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1998|1998]], and became the first candidate to win a majority of the popular vote for a first term since [[Kenneth M. Curtis]] defeated incumbent governor [[John H. Reed]] in [[Maine gubernatorial election, 1966|1966]], though Curtis and Reed were the only candidates in that race.
